title: Ecommerce growth: product pages and retention
summary: Find where buyers drop out before choosing what to change.
why: Fix purchase barriers before paying for more traffic.
Margin, refunds and repeat purchases give a clearer view of growth than revenue alone.
know: Check the view-to-cart-to-checkout-to-purchase funnel by source, device and market. Validate tracking first.
Product pages must explain specifications, fit, delivery, returns and trust. Claims and reviews must be real.
Consider margin, stock, service cost and opt-outs when planning discounts, subscriptions and retention.
inputs: Funnel, product and margin data; support and return reasons
Campaign rules, stock, audience consent and brand assets
actions: Inspect funnel losses and valuable products. Rank hypotheses by impact and evidence.
Draft changes to product pages, offers or retention flows. Fix functional and data issues first.
Define the main metric, guardrails, observation period and sample interpretation.
done: Purchase and refund paths work; events and revenue reconcile reasonably.
Conclusions state sample limits and distinguish seasonal or promotional effects from causation.
pitfalls: Watching ROAS while ignoring margin, refunds and new customers.
Declaring a winner before enough data is available.
decision: Agree on offers, minimum margin and the funnel stage to improve first.

reader.concept: Ecommerce growth means finding losses between arrival and repeat purchase, then improving the stage with the greatest impact.
reader.when: Use this when traffic fails to convert, campaigns weaken or repeat sales need work.

example.situation: Many shoppers leave after adding to cart because shipping costs appear only at checkout.
example.lesson: Locate the drop-off before proposing a testable change.

reader.first_step: Inspect the funnel for one main market and device.
